transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, nice to meet you, Doctor. I guess I came in because... well, it's my husband’s sister. She has been working this family business so she can get control of the money and just completely push me out of decisions. And no matter how folks try to smooth it over, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now. 

Which, you know, a year ago was right around the time the county came and dug up the road in front of our house. They said it was for the water lines, but they left a giant dirt hole there for weeks. Just orange cones everywhere. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he actually backed his truck right into one of the ditches because he wasn't looking. He’s got that old blue Ford, the one with the rust on the tailgate, and it took a tow truck two hours to pull him out of there. I watched the whole thing from my porch. 

But anyway, I don't know why everyone keeps making excuses for her when it's plain as day what she's trying to do to me with the money.
Aside from your concerns about your sister-in-law, have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people don't seem to notice?

No, nothing like that. I don't hear voices or see ghosts or whatever. I mean, I hear plenty of actual noise, like that stray dog that barks at all hours of the night. I think it belongs to the folks two streets over, the ones who moved in right around Halloween. 

I remember it was Halloween because they put up one of those giant inflatable pumpkins in their front yard, and it got a hole in it the very first week. It just laid there in the grass looking like a flat orange pancake for a month. I don't know why people buy those inflatable things anyway, they must use up so much electricity to keep them blown up. My electric bill went up twenty dollars last month just from running the little space heater out in the sunroom, and I only turn that on in the mornings when I'm drinking my coffee. It gets awful drafty out there since the weather turned. But no, I don't hear anything that isn't really there.
Over this past year, have you had any extended periods where your mood was unusually low, or alternatively, unusually elevated or full of energy, separate from your feelings about your sister-in-law?

Well, no, not really. I'm just my regular self, you know? I don't get all depressed or start bouncing off the walls or anything like that. I just have my normal amount of energy. 

Which, speaking of energy, I was actually trying to use some to clean out the hall closet on Tuesday, and I found this heavy old box of my husband's bowling trophies. He used to bowl in that Thursday night league over at Pinewood Lanes before they closed the whole place down and turned it into that giant discount furniture store. We went in there once to look for a recliner, but everything they sell is that cheap particle board stuff. You know the kind, where you put a glass of ice water down on it and the wood just bubbles right up and ruins it. My cousin bought a TV stand from a place like that and the whole thing completely collapsed when her husband tried to slide it over to vacuum. Broke their good flat-screen television right smack in half. They had to fight with the store manager for a month to get their money back. 

But anyway, what were we saying? Oh, right. No, my mood has been perfectly fine, nothing unusual.

Have you been diagnosed with any medical or neurological conditions—like thyroid problems, seizures, head injury, or been using any medications, alcohol, or recreational drugs—around the time these beliefs about your sister-in-law started?

No, I haven't had any of that. No seizures, no thyroid issues, and I don't do any drugs or drink. I just take my daily vitamins. I get those gummy ones from the pharmacy down on Main Street. The pharmacist there, Brenda, she's been working there since my kids were little. She has this granddaughter who just started kindergarten, and Brenda was showing me pictures of her on her phone the other day. She had her hair in these little pigtails with pink ribbons, just cute as a button. 

It made me think about when my daughter was that age, she refused to wear anything but purple for a whole year. Purple shirts, purple pants, even these little purple sparkly shoes. We had to go to three different shoe stores at the mall just to find them in her size. That was back when the mall still had that big fountain in the center where people would throw pennies in. They took it out a few years ago and put in one of those little kiosks that sells phone cases. It's a shame, really, the fountain was so pretty. 

But anyway, no, I haven't had any head injuries or anything medical going on. I'm healthy as a horse.
Aside from the tension with your sister-in-law, has this past year affected your ability to keep up with your usual daily routines, work, or relationships with other people?

Well, no, my day-to-day is pretty much the exact same as it's always been. I still go to my quilting group on Tuesdays, and choir practice on Wednesday nights. And I've been keeping up with my GED lessons, plus my senior walks at the park in the mornings. 

Speaking of the park, they just put in these new benches over by the duck pond. They're that recycled plastic material that's supposed to look like wood, but you can tell it's not. I was sitting on one last week after my walk, and this woman came by with a Golden Retriever that decided to shake itself dry right next to me. Got my good walking shoes all muddy. I had to scrub them with an old toothbrush when I got home. I use this special soap my neighbor makes—she melts down leftover slivers of bar soap and mixes them with lavender oil. It smells real nice, but she always leaves these little gift baskets on my porch and I honestly have more soap than I know what to do with now. I gave three bars to my mailman for Christmas. He seemed a little confused, but it's the thought that counts, right? 

But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, right, my routines. Yeah, they're fine. Really, the only thing that's changed is how much I trust my husband's sister. I just have to be real careful about which family gatherings I go to now, because I never know what she's going to pull. But other than that, everything is just fine.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a single, fixed, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (belief that sister-in-law is manipulating family finances to exclude her) persisting for over one year. There are no hallucinations, no manic or depressive episodes, no negative symptoms, and no evidence of substance use or medical/neurological etiology. Functioning is preserved across social, occupational (GED classes), and recreational domains (quilting, choir, walking group), with impairment isolated to interactions concerning the sister-in-law. Speech is circumstantial/tangential with excessive irrelevant detail, but this is a feature of communication style rather than formal thought disorder, and the delusion itself remains organized and non-bizarre. This presentation is most consistent with Delusional Disorder (F22) rather than Schizophrenia (which requires additional psychotic symptoms or functional decline) or a mood disorder with psychotic features (no mood episode present).
